sweep_summary: Huichol (huic1243) is not in the catalog. The single stress-title item, Banerji 2014/2015 (BA thesis, handle 10066/15903), was already held by the project and was re-read in full: it argues Huichol has lexically underlying, unpredictable, obligatory and culminative word accent, one accented mora per prosodic word, realized as privative high tone (tone-accent language), with minimal pairs tame/tamé, ne?ena/ne?ená, naka/náka; it also relays Iturrioz et al. 1999 (grammatical vs lexical stress accent, penultimate stress kept under suffixation) and Grimes 1959 (stress derived from pitch and foot structure, default first syllable). Corroborating first-hand statement held by the project: McIntosh 1945 IJAL 11:31-32, 'Stress is phonemic.. the majority of the words, but by no means all of them, have the last stress in the word on the penult.' Grimes 1981 (tone on every syllable, foot stress derived from tones and lengths) and Pharao Hansen 2024 (secondary synthesis: lexical pitch-related accent) also held by the project. Suggested coding for a new record: lexical/contrastive accent with penultimate as the common default. Not obtainable by automated download (already recorded): Grimes 1959 IJAL 25:221-232 (doi:10.1086/464536, paywalled), Iturrioz, Ramírez & Pacheco 1999 Gramática didáctica del huichol I (print), Iturrioz & Gómez 2006 Gramática wixarika I (print), Gómez López 1999 Huichol de San Andrés Cohamiata (print). the handle record was verified by download. updated at

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress (accent) is contrastive: its position distinguishes otherwise identical words, so it must be lexically specified; the last (main) stress of a word nevertheless falls on the penultimate syllable in the majority of words, with final stress arising when an inherently unstressable morpheme occupies the penult, and additional (earlier) stresses tied to particular morphemes in long polysynthetic words. Later work agrees on the contrastiveness and the penultimate default (Iturrioz et al. 1999, second-hand) but Grimes (1959, 1981, 2008) reanalyses the system as lexical high/low tone with stress derived from tone, length and foot structure, and Banerji (2015) as one lexically accented mora per word bearing H tone (tone-accent).
new_statements.secondary_stress: McIntosh speaks of 'other stresses in the word' (besides the last stress) whose presence depends on which morphemes are present -- some morphemes are generally stressed, others seldom or never; no rhythmic rule given. Grimes 1981 instead divides long words into rhythmic feet each with one stress.
new_statements.exceptions: Words whose last stress is not penultimate ('by no means all of them'); final stress when an unstressable morpheme is penult; minimal pairs 'tuka/tu'ka, '?aki/?a'ki, pʌ'waki/pʌwa'ki. (Iturrioz et al. 1999, per Banerji: grammatical accent shifts under suffixation e.g. máxa -> maxátsi, tsíki -> tsiikíri, and lexical pairs tuutú/tútu-type; Banerji: Spanish loans keep penultimate accent.)
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level statement based on isolated words and short utterances from La Piedra Gorda (Nayarit) speakers, 1941-43; McIntosh treats stress as a suprasegmental phoneme of the word. Grimes 1959/1981 relocate the domain to the rhythmic foot and intonation group; Banerji 2015 to the lexical word (one accent per word, elicited in isolation, with a caveat about prepausal/isolation effects).
new_statements.identity_note: McIntosh 1945 describes the speech of La Piedra Gorda (about 50 mi east of Tepic, Nayarit; eastern Huichol), recorded 1941-43. Grimes 1981 and the 1954/1996 vocabulario are ILV work centred on the eastern (Santa Catarina, Jal.) and central dialects. Banerji 2015 used one consultant (Diego Carrillo Robles) recorded in Mexico City plus published data, and himself notes that Grimes's 1959 dialect differs (has /q/, /z/). The modern reference descriptions (Iturrioz et al. 1999; Iturrioz & Gómez López 2006; Gómez López 1999) are based mainly on San Andrés Cohamiata and neighbouring Jalisco communities. All are Huichol, glottocode huic1243; Glottolog lists no dialect sub-codes.

new_statements.quote: In summary, I have shown in this section that Huichol has lexically underlying, distinctive, and unpredictable word accent, and that tone in Huichol is borne by the mora, rather than the syllable. I have further confirmed that Huichol accent is both obligatory and culminative, thus satisfying the two main necessary conditions for being analyzed as accent, rather than tone.
new_statements.citation: Banerji, Robindra Nath. 2014 [2015]. Huichol (Wixarika) Word Accent: Typology, Interactions, and Implications. B.A. thesis, Haverford/Swarthmore (Tri-College), advisor B. D. Lillehaugen.http://hdl.handle.net/10066/15903
new_statements.locator: p. 28 (end of §4.3), with Abstract p. 1 and minimal pairs §4.1 pp. 22-24
new_statements.reading: Lexical (unpredictable) word accent: exactly one accented mora per prosodic word, realized as high tone; contrastive position shown by minimal pairs (tame 'tooth' vs tamé 'we'; ne?ena present vs ne?ená future; naka 'ear' vs náka). Spanish loans and several native examples show penultimate accent as the common but not rule-governed position, which matches the older first-hand statement of McIntosh 1945 (IJAL 11: 31-32, also held by the project): stress is phonemic, and the last stress falls on the penult in the majority but by no means all words, with other stresses morpheme-determined. Grimes (1959, 1981) instead derives stress from tone and syllable length within feet. Best coding for a catalog entry: lexical/unpredictable accent (pitch-realized), penultimate as the statistical default, not fixed. Caveats: BA thesis, one consultant, dialect differs from Grimes'.

new_statements.quote: Wixárika also creates lexical contrast with stress like other Uto-Aztecan languages, shown in (10). (10) Lexical contrast with first and second syllable stress a. tá:me 'we/nosotros' b. ta:mé 'tooth/diente' c. múme 'beans/frijoles' d. mumé 'kidney/riñón' [Elicit] || [p. 45, reporting the orthography adopted:] Iturrioz et al. (1999) proposed double vowel graphemes to represent length, in addition to creating accent rules: 1. Accents in the penultimate syllable will not be marked (máxa=maxa 'deer/venado'; tumíni=tumini 'money/dinero'). 2. Accents in syllables other than the penultimate will be marked ('ukí='ukí 'man/hombre'; 'ukári='ukári 'woman/mujer'). ... 5. Monosyllabic words that occur in minimal pairs will be accented to avoid ambiguities ('aki 'river/río', 'akí 'your house/tu casa')

new_statements.relation_note: Same type as the existing statements (McIntosh 1945: stress phonemic, last stress mostly on the penult; Banerji 2015: lexical, unpredictable word accent with penult as the frequent position). Adds two elicited minimal pairs and documents the Iturrioz et al. (1999) penult-default orthographic convention. The catalog record itself has an empty rule, so nothing to contradict. Minor data point: Ramos Bierge glosses tá:me 'we' / ta:mé 'tooth'; the project's earlier summary of Banerji listed the pair as tame 'tooth' vs tamé 'we' (Banerji's scanned text held by the project has lost the diacritics, so that assignment cannot be checked here); this does not affect the reading. Corpus draws on several…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress (accent) is lexically contrastive: disyllables with identical segments differ only in whether stress is on the first or second syllable (tá:me 'we' vs ta:mé 'tooth'; múme 'beans' vs mumé 'kidney'). The dissertation gives no placement rule of its own; the orthography it adopts (Iturrioz et al. 1999) treats penultimate accent as the unmarked default and writes an acute only when the accent falls elsewhere, which implies penult is the common position but not predictable.
new_statements.exceptions: None as such; the phonology overview is brief (the work is a morphosyntax dissertation). It notes McIntosh (1945) described accent and Grimes (1959) tone and intonation, without taking a position on tone vs stress. Orthographic rule 3: after derivation the marking rules re-apply to the new word ('ukí vs 'ukiyari), rule 6: accent shifted outside the lexical word is marked.
new_statements.identity_note: Ramos Bierge's corpus mixes speakers of several Wixárika dialects (mainly Jalisco and Nayarit, to a lesser extent Zacatecas; ch. 1 p. ~10 and ch. 2 sec. on dialects); the phonology sketch is presented for the language as a whole and the data are written in the Iturrioz et al. (1999) orthography.

sources.quote: Cora and Huichol have both been described as having a lexical accent that is somehow related to pitch, whereas Nahuan varieties spoken today generally have a fixed stress system with stress falling on the penultimate syllable of the word. ... There have been various interpretations of accent and tone in Huichol. Descriptions of Huichol tend to mark accent, because it is required to distinguish minimal pairs such as tamé ... táme ... Banerji (2014) gives a contrary analysis of Huichol as having lexical pitch accent in which high tone ... In synthesis, the evidence suggests that Huichol words can carry more than one high tone, and that it is a question of analysis whether this is best understood as pitch accent with floating tones, or as a tonal system in which tone is assigned lexically to every syllable.
sources.locator: §2.2 'Accent in Uto-Aztecan and in Cora, Huichol and Nahua' (accepted manuscript, unpaginated text)
sources.note: Second-hand survey (sec. 2.2): Cora and Huichol described as having lexical accent related to pitch; Grimes (1959, 2008) treats Huichol as tonal (every syllable H or L; stress from interaction of tone, vowel length and foot boundaries) whereas Banerji (2014) analyses lexical pitch accent with H on the accented mora; 'it is a question of analysis' which is right; minimal pairs tamé/táme, múme/mumé cited.

sources.note: Own fieldwork (one consultant) + published data: Huichol is an accentual (tone-accent) language with exactly one lexically underlying, distinctive, unpredictable accented mora per word; accented moras receive privative H tone; mora is TBU; minimal pairs by accent position (táme 'tooth' vs tamé 'we'; náka vs naká) and grammatical H-tone shift (present vs future). Reviews McIntosh 1945, Grimes 1959 (four-level intonation contours + derived stress), Grimes 2008, and reports Iturrioz, Ramírez & Pacheco 1999:55,147,153 as treating Huichol as a stress language with lexical vs grammatical stress acc…

sources.quote: In summary, I have shown in this section that Huichol has lexically underlying, distinctive, and unpredictable word accent, and that tone in Huichol is borne by the mora, rather than the syllable. I have further confirmed that Huichol accent is both obligatory and culminative, thus satisfying the two main necessary conditions for being analyzed as accent, rather than tone. (p. 28) ... Huichol is an accentual language with one accented mora per word. Huichol has privative tone that interacts with the accentual system: accented moras are assigned high tone. Thus, Huichol should be classified as a tone-accent language. (Abstract, p. 1)
sources.locator: Abstract p. 1; §3.2 'Stress in Huichol' pp. 20-22; §4.1 pp. 22-24 (minimal pairs); §4.3 pp. 26-28 (obligatory + culminative); App. 1 p. 34 (Grimes 1959 stress rules)
sources.note: Word accent is lexical and unpredictable: one accented mora per prosodic word, realized as H tone (privative H vs no tone); minimal pairs from one Tuapurie/Santa Catarina speaker in Mexico City: tame 'tooth' vs tamé 'we', ne?ena 'I hear' vs ne?ená 'I will hear' (penultimate vs final H), naka 'ear' vs náka (Spanish loan). Spanish loans wakaxi 'cow', kapura 'goat' take penultimate accent. Accent is obligatory and culminative; some affixes (e.g. -ratsih) delete root accent, others keep it; tense markers analysed as floating H docking to the final mora, giving surface words with two H's. Reports…

sources.citation: Grimes, Joseph E. (with P. de la Cruz Avila et al.) 1981. El huichol: apuntes sobre el léxico. Ithaca, NY: Dept. of Modern Languages and Linguistics, Cornell University. (ERIC ED210901)
sources.quote: Muchas palabras son partidas en dos o más secuencias rítmicas de sílabas, cada una con las características fonológicas (pero no las gramaticales) de una palabra sola, o más bien dicho de un pie métrico. Cada secuencia tiene un acento que es determinado por la serie de tonos y por la duración de las sílabas que la componen. [English version p. 286:] Many words consist of two or more rhythmic feet, groups of syllables united around a stressed syllable. The stress is derived from the arrangement of tones and syllable lengths, and in some cases from the specific consonants and vowels involved.
sources.locator: Introducción, 'Ortografía' (p. 4 of the Spanish introduction); English 'Writing System' note, p. 286
sources.note: Introducción p.7 'Ortografía' and English summary p.286: every syllable carries high tone (acute accent) or low tone (unmarked); words divide into rhythmic feet, each with one stress ('acento') that is determined by the sequence of tones and syllable lengths (CVV = long), sometimes by the segments; foot division does not follow morpheme division. No fixed stress position stated.

sources.note: A synchronic sketch of Huichol phonology in 12 numbered traits (no voiced obstruents, no l/r opposition, s as allophone of ts, 5 vowel qualities without o/u contrast, i as epenthetic vowel, CV(V) syllable canon, no clusters or codas, two glottal consonants, no vowel-initial syllables, contrastive vowel length with minimal pairs ha:xi/haxi, te:wi/tewi, tu:tú/tutú, i u vs y w), consonant and vowel charts, vowel sequences and diphthongs ('Grimes no constata la existencia de las mismas'), then Nahuatl and Mexican Spanish inventories for contrast. It contains NO statement on Huichol accent, stress…
